A Computational Study of Belief, Surprise, and Structural Inference Under Uncertainty

This documentation accompanies the TAMBI research project, which investigates how humans infer latent environmental structure under different levels of task ambiguity, and how evolving beliefs guide spatio-temporal action under uncertainty. The study integrates a custom behavioral task, multi-modal physiological recording and multiple questionnaires covering mental health, focusing anxiety. A family of 15 particle-filter based agent models provide a tangible representation of how differences in prior knowledge, cognitive capabilities and decision-making preferences shape behavior in our task. Building up on that, we use armortized bayesian inference to extract four individual parameters that reflect the underlying trait-level differences in behavioral patterns. By correlating(?) these parameters with the questionnaire scores, individual task performace differences and related affective reactions, we build a unified framework for the investigation of how mental health profiles are linked to learning and inference in uncertain dynamic environments.

This book is organized into five major parts:

Theoretical Background
A concise review of the conceptual foundations motivating the project: the decomposition of uncertainty into epistemic and aleatoric components, the active inference framework, and the computational mechanisms by which trait anxiety is hypothesized to distort inference and learning.

The Experiment
A full description of the experimental design, the Mosquito Defense task, the trial schedule generation procedure, and the PsychoPy implementation. This section covers the three instruction conditions, the gamification layer, and the multi-modal data streams collected during testing.

The Simulation Models
Detailed specifications for all 15 computational models, organized into four conceptual groups: baseline models, core Bayesian inference models, temporal commitment models, and rule-knowledge models. This section also covers the shared model architecture (particle filter, action selection, cost function), implementation details, and simulation results.

Participant Data Analysis
Preprocessing and analysis pipelines for behavioral, eye-tracking, pupil, mouse-tracking, and heart rate data. Includes the post-experiment questionnaire analysis.

Computational Model Fitting
The Amortized Bayesian Inference procedure for participant-level parameter inference, including parameter recovery, and identifiability analyses.

The core experimental paradigm - the Mosquito Defense Task - requires participants to allocate a fixed budget of seven nets across 32 angular slots surrounding a central target, in order to intercept probabilistic mosquito attacks. The direction of each attack is governed by latent contextual states and color cues, according to rules that participants may or may not be explicitly taught (depending on instruction condition). Episodes of approximately 20 trials (16-24) each are separated by unannounced rotations of the entire cue-outcome mapping.

The task is designed to place varying demands on:

Cue-contingency learning - learning which color predicts which direction

Latent state inference - tracking which of two rotated contexts is currently active

Uncertainty decomposition - distinguishing irreducible outcome noise from genuine structural change

Fifteen particle-filter-based computational models varying systematically in representational capacity, inferential mechanisms, and prior knowledge are simulated on the task to identify different related behavioral patterns. The models span the range from a memoryless Markov baseline to an oracle agent with complete structural knowledge, with the primary scientific interest lying in the intermediate inference models and how structural priors impact their behavior.

Using Amortized Bayesian Inference we estimate four participant-level parameters that reflect
By mapping the individual parameter values on questionnaire scores and physiological measures, this approach allows to investigate how individual differences in model parameters relate to trait anxiety and other individual difference variables.

This chapter documents the analysis layer that connects the three data streams the project produces about each participant: the behavioural data (and its GLMM-derived summaries), the BayesFlow-inferred computational parameters, and the questionnaire scores. The three connection-level chapters — 

Symptom → Behaviour, 

Symptom → Parameters, and 

Parameters ↔ Behaviour — cross-reference back to the shared design decisions documented here, in the same way the behavioural model chapters reference 

Cross Cutting Methods.

The shared foundation is implemented in integration_common.py; the three connection-level analyses are symptom_behavior_models.py, symptom_parameter_models.py, and parameter_behavior_models.py.

By the time a participant has been through the pipeline, three quite different descriptions of them exist. The behavioural pipeline (

Primary GLMMs, and the raw descriptive markers) yields summary statistics and a handful of GLMM-derived per-participant scalars (cue-dissociation rate, evidence-dependence slope, rule-applier class, discovery episode, the Rule-1 marker). The amortized inference pipeline (

The Inference Agent, 

Amortized Bayesian Inference) yields six parameter posteriors per participant. The questionnaire pipeline yields the trait and symptom scales.

Each of these was, until this layer was added, analysed largely in isolation. The integration layer closes that gap and merges the seperate data streams in a single place and under one coherent methodological umbrella. It exists to answer three families of question:

Do symptoms predict behaviour? - 

Symptom → Behaviour.

Do symptoms predict the computational parameters? - 

Symptom → Parameters.

Do the computational parameters track the behaviour they are meant to, and do they mediate any symptom→behaviour link? (construct validity and mechanism) - 

Parameters ↔ Behaviour.

Within the integration pipeline, all three connection-level scripts obtain their data from a single function, integration_common.build_master_table, which assembles one per-participant table from whatever streams are available. This was implemented to prevent that each script re-implements its own merge, with its own ID matching and its own column conventions.

Stream

Source

Contents

Instruction condition

behavioural results

the ordered condition factor + its condition_L / condition_Q contrasts

Model-independent features

feature_extraction.py

the 54 features (allocation shape, oddball/transition/omission reaction, cue differentiation, dynamics)

Behavioural summary

build_behavioral_summary

defense rate, angular error, entropy, placement speed, state-affect means/slopes

GLMM-derived scalars

statistical-analysis output dir

cue-dissociation rate, evidence-dependence slope, rule-applier class, discovery episode, Rule-1 marker

BayesFlow parameters

the six parameter posterior means and per-parameter posterior SDs

Questionnaire scores

Every stream is optional except the behavioural results, which anchor participant identity and the instruction condition. Streams that are absent are simply omitted; the table contains whatever could be assembled. The condition contrasts are reconstructed here using the same orthogonal-polynomial coding documented in 

Cross Cutting Methods, so that condition moderation tests in the integration layer are coded identically to the behavioural GLMMs.

The original design envisaged consuming the GLMM random-effect BLUPs (per-participant slopes for oddball reactivity, transition reactivity, generalisation, and so on) as the individual-difference measures linking behaviour to the other layers — this is the approach documented in 

Factor Structure.

At the current N, however, every model in the behavioural pipeline falls back to ols_cluster_robust or mixedlm_full without an estimable random-effect covariance, so no M*_blups.csv files are produced. The integration layer therefore builds on the GLMM-derived scalar outputs instead (cue-dissociation rate, evidence-dependence slope, rule-applier class, discovery episode, the Rule-1 marker) which are computed directly and do not depend on a random-effect structure being estimable. The harvest routine will pick up M*_blups.csv automatically if they ever appear (e.g. at the target N, when models (hopefully) converge with random slopes), with no code change required.

The current N is small (≈34) and the target is N ≈ 90–100. Corrections are therefore deliberately light-touch, on the reasoning that effects which are marginal at the current N are expected to firm up toward the target rather than to be artefacts, and over-correcting now would discard them prematurely and thus complicating the preliminary interpretation within the data collection phase. Concretely:

Primary families: small sets of theory-motivated, directional tests (e.g. H1 anxiety → noise_reactivity; the parameter↔behaviour convergent-validity pairings). These are corrected, if at all, within their own small family using Holm (family-wise control is the appropriate frame for a handful of directional primary tests), and are reported uncorrected alongside.

Exploratory grids: the full trait × metric and parameter × feature matrices. These get Benjamini–Hochberg FDR and are labelled explicitly as hypothesis-generating.

Every correction in the code carries an inline comment stating which family it belongs to and why. The aim is that a reader (and myself whenever I come back to the code in the future) can always tell whether a reported effect came from a small directional family or from a large exploratory grid.

The internalizing scales are strongly inter-correlated (trait anxiety, intolerance of uncertainty, depression, emotion-regulation difficulty all load on a shared internalizing dimension; the pairwise correlations in this sample run roughly 0.5–0.8). This is expected and is consistent with the broader literature, but it has a direct methodological consequence for this layer, since bivariate trait → parameter and trait → behaviour correlations are not, on their own, interpretable as evidence for a specific trait, because the shared internalizing variance is attributed to whichever scale is entered.

The integration scripts therefore report partial correlations (each trait controlling for the others) alongside the bivariate results, and the partial results should be treated as the more informative readout when asking whether a specific construct drives an association vs. a more general, potentially transdiagnostic factor. See 

Symptom → Parameters for a worked example where a bivariate-null association (trait anxiety → noise_reactivity) becomes the strongest signal in the table once the shared internalizing variance is partialled out.

This chapter documents the analysis that links the BayesFlow-inferred parameters to the behavioural data, on two levels, with statistical models rather than correlations and visualisation alone (the latter being what behavioral_validation.py already provides). It is implemented in parameter_behavior_models.py and draws its data from the canonical master table described in 

Cross-layer Integration: Overview.

The chapter answers two questions. First, construct validity: does each inferred parameter track the behavioural signature it is meant to, in the direction the generative model implies? Second, mechanism: does a parameter mediate any symptom → behaviour relationship?

Every prediction in this chapter is anchored to the parameter semantics defined in 

The Inference Agent. Two of the six parameters have a direction that is easy to invert, and inverting it turns a confirmation into an apparent contradiction:

Two parameters whose behavioural direction is counter-intuitive

noise_reactivity: high values mean surprises (i.e. oddballs) are attributed to noise, which produces weaker learning from oddballs and therefore a smaller oddball-driven behavioural shift. (Low values attribute surprises to state change → strong learning → larger shift.) So higher noise_reactivity predicts a smaller oddball shift.

belief_momentum: high values mean inertia in latent-state inference: sluggish adaptation, slow state switching. So higher belief_momentum predicts a smaller and slower post-transition belief revision, not a faster one.

Level A regresses each behavioural feature on each parameter (participant-level OLS, standardised, controlling for condition), across the full feature set: the 54 features from feature_extraction.py plus the summary and GLMM-derived metrics used in the behavioural pipeline. The grid is corrected with Benjamini–Hochberg FDR as an exploratory family.

The dominant Level A pattern in the current data is that precision_weighting and belief_momentum load on overlapping allocation-shape and tracking features, with opposite signs:

precision_weighting → low entropy, high stacking, few slots occupied (β up to ±0.84).

belief_momentum → high tracking error, high circular variance, low cue-dissociation, smaller post-transition shift.

This opposite-sign pattern is expected, not an identifiability problem

A participant with high precision_weighting (concentrates the allocation tightly) and low belief_momentum (switches state readily when reversal evidence accumulates) is a tight, agile, structure-using learner; the opposite participant is diffuse and sluggish. These are opposite ends of two distinct parameters that nonetheless co-vary across participants because cognitive / learning phenotypes load on both. The parameters control genuinely different behavioural signatures, confirmed by the parameter-recovery sweeps documented in 

The Inference Agent and model_behavior_extended.py, which show clean, separable recovery and distinct behavioural effects when each parameter is varied with the others held fixed. The correlation seen here is therefore a property of the participants (a real phenotype covariance), not of the inference (parameter confusion).

Each pairing is tested by Spearman correlation with a one-sided p in the predicted direction and a within-family Holm flag. Holm is applied only within this small primary family, not folded into the Level A exploratory grid.

The last three pairings are the convergent-validity checks for the two parameters added after the original four. They are different in spirit from the symptom-driven hypotheses. Rather than testing a clinical prediction, they ask whether each new parameter does, behaviourally, what the model says it does. cue_sensitivity should manifest as a larger learned cue offset and cleaner cue dissociation, since that is precisely the associative quantity it scales, and placement_noise should manifest as greater undirected within-state scatter, since that is the action-level variability it was introduced to absorb. These are the most direct behavioural footprints any of the parameters have, so they serve as a sanity check on the inference as much as a substantive finding.

h_switch is the parameter with the weakest behavioural grounding here, since it acts on the timescale of the latent-state belief trajectory (z_prob drift), which does not map cleanly onto any single static summary feature the way the other three parameters do. Its convergent-validity pairings are correspondingly the most tentative.

The final module asks whether a parameter mediates a symptom → behaviour relationship. For a small set of theory-motivated triples (ADD LIST), it estimates the standard product-of-coefficients indirect effect with a bias-corrected bootstrap confidence interval, on standardised variables. This complements the trait → state → behaviour mediation already in behavior_questionnaire_integration.py by putting the computational parameter in the mediator role.

This chapter documents the models that use questionnaire (trait / symptom) scores as predictors of behavioural metrics, which is the most direct analysis level for the internalizing and anxiety hypotheses. It is implemented in symptom_behavior_models.py and draws its data from the master table described in 

Cross-layer Integration: Overview.

What this integration layer contributes is proper regression with covariate control, condition moderation, both a participant-level (two-stage) and a trial-level (hierarchical) route, and outcome-appropriate models for the categorical and temporal behavioural targets.

The behavioural outcomes fall into three families:

Model-independent summary metrics, namely defense rate, mean angular error, net entropy, placement speed; one continuous value per participant.

GLMM-derived per-participant scalars, namely cue-dissociation rate, evidence-dependence slope, the Rule-1 marker (post-transition belief shift). These are the individual-difference measures distilled by the behavioural pipeline (see 

Primary GLMMs).

Categorical / temporal outcomes, which include the rule-applier class (modelled by logistic regression) and discovery episode (related to traits by rank correlation, given the small applier subsample)

For every (trait, target) pair, two participant-level OLS models are fit on standardised variables:target ~ trait                          [+ covariates]      (main effect)
target ~ trait * condition_L            [+ covariates]      (moderation)

The first asks whether the trait predicts the behavioural metric; the second asks whether that relationship is moderated by instruction depth (a trait : condition_L interaction). Covariates (age, sex) are included when present in the merged table. The full trait x target grid of main-effect tests is corrected with Benjamini–Hochberg FDR as an exploratory family; the interaction tests are corrected as a separate family because they answer a different question. Both the main-effect and interaction FDR families are flagged hypothesis-generating.

Why both a two-stage and a hierarchical route

The two-stage approach collapses each participant to one summary value and is transparent and robust. The hierarchical approach uses all trials and a participant random intercept, which is more powerful but heavier and, importantly, requires care in interpretation when the predictor of interest varies only between participants. The two are offered together so they can be read against each other.

For a small set of headline trial-level outcomes (angular_error_deg, defense_rate), the script additionally fits a mixed model with the trait as a between-participant (level-2) predictor:trial_outcome ~ trait_z + condition_L + (1 | participant)

using mixedlm for the Gaussian outcome and BinomialBayesMixedGLM (variational Bayes) for the per-trial binary outcome. These fit where feasible and record their fit method and convergence; some are tight at the current N and fall back gracefully.

Interpreting the hierarchical fixed effects

When a between-participant predictor (a trait, constant within participant) is entered into a trial-level mixed model with thousands of trials, the standard error on that predictor can be driven down by trial-level variance that is unrelated to the between-participant contrast, producing implausibly small p-values. In the current run with N = 34, the hierarchical defense_rate models returned highly “significant” trait effects (e.g. IU → defense rate, p < 10⁻⁵) that are entirely absent from the two-stage analysis on the same data. Where the two routes disagree this sharply, the two-stage estimate is the honest readout of the between-participant relationship, and the hierarchical fixed effect should be treated with suspicion until the random-effect structure has been checked (e.g. confirming the trait coefficient is stable when the model is reduced to a random intercept only). The hierarchical models are retained for the headline outcomes but are not, at present, the basis for any between-participant trait claim.

Rule-applier class is reduced to a binary indicator (immediate or late applier = 1) and modelled by logistic regression on each trait, controlling for condition:rule_applier_is_applier ~ trait_z + condition_L

This asks whether a trait raises or lowers the odds of applying the structural rule, over and above the instruction manipulation. The exploratory family is FDR-corrected.

Discovery episode (when an applier first reliably applies the rule) is related to traits by Spearman correlation, restricted to the applier subsample. This is the analysis that speaks to the hypothesis that a stronger tendency to find patterns may come with earlier discovery (and may relate to mental-health measures). It is deliberately not FDR-corrected, since at the pilot N the applier subsample is tiny (often well under ten) but might still be insightful to already investigate to eventually control for interactions in future analyses, so this is purely descriptive / hypothesis-generating and is flagged as such, to be revisited at the target N.

At N = 32 the two-stage main effects are uniformly modest and none survive FDR, which is obviously not suprising. However, the value of running this layer now is in establishing the pipeline and the operationalisations, not in the any point estimates.

This chapter documents the models that use questionnaire (trait / symptom) scores as predictors of the BayesFlow-inferred computational parameters. It is implemented in symptom_parameter_models.py and draws its data from the canonical master table described in 

Cross-layer Integration: Overview.

What this integration layer contributes is regression with covariate control, condition moderation, partial correlations, and parameter-uncertainty weighting, organised around a small set of theory-motivated primary hypotheses (to be discussed!).

The parameters and their semantics are defined fully in 

The Inference Agent; they are summarised here only insofar as the directional hypotheses depend on getting their meaning exactly right.

The agent has six parameters in total, but the symptom-driven hypotheses concern only the four original ones, listed below. The two parameters added later, cue_sensitivity and placement_noise, were mainly introduced for reasons internal to the model (isolating associative cue learning and absorbing undirected within-state placement scatter, respectively) and neither carries an a-priori clinical prediction (to be discussed - however, the prediction would not be a priori atp). cue_sensitivity is in fact expected to eventually dissociate from the internalizing scales (it indexes a learning ability rather than an affective bias), and placement_noise is an execution-noise term. Both are still entered into the exploratory trait x parameter grid further down, but they do not appear among the primary hypotheses, and the current empirical results (N = 34) bear this out: neither shows a meaningful correlation with any questionnaire scale.

Parameter

Meaning

Direction that matters

precision_weighting

allocation concentration / stacking

high → tighter, more concentrated placement

noise_reactivity

stochasticity-attribution bias (Piray & Daw)

high → surprises attributed to noise → weaker learning

belief_momentum

inertia in latent-state inference

high → sluggish state switching

h_switch

perceived environmental volatility

high → readier to entertain a state change

The two emphasised rows are the ones whose direction is counter-intuitive from the name alone, and getting them backwards inverts every downstream prediction - a clarification worth stating explicitly here because it is easy to get confused here (this is of course not stated because it is driven by my own experience - would never happen to me for sure).

records.content:
The three primary hypotheses

H1 (Piray & Daw, 2021): trait anxiety (STICSA-T) → lower noise_reactivity. Anxious participants over-attribute surprising outcomes to genuine structural change rather than to noise, i.e. they have a lower noise-attribution setting.

H2 (Zika et al., 2023): intolerance of uncertainty (IU-18) → higher belief_momentum. Difficulty tolerating uncertainty manifests as reluctance to commit to a stable state belief, i.e. sluggish, inertial state inference.

H3 (volatility over-estimation): intolerance of uncertainty → higher h_switch. Over-estimation of how often the environment changes.

Each is a single directional prediction, tested with a Spearman correlation, a two-sided p, a one-sided p in the predicted direction, and a within-family Holm flag. Holm (family-wise) is applied only within this three-member family, since these are the primary tests and are not folded into the exploratory grid, which would over-penalise them at current N (to be discussed how to adjust this at final N).

For every (trait, parameter) pair the script fits, on standardised variables:parameter ~ trait                       [+ covariates]      (main effect)
parameter ~ trait * condition_L         [+ covariates]      (moderation)

and, where a posterior SD column ({param}_std) is available, a precision-weighted main-effect model with weights 1/\text{SD}^2, so that participants whose parameter is poorly identified contribute less. The weighted estimate is reported alongside the unweighted one. The full main-effect grid is FDR-corrected as an exploratory family.

Because the internalizing scales are strongly inter-correlated (see 

overview), the script computes partial Spearman correlations between each anxiety-core trait and each parameter, controlling for the other core traits. This separates the unique contribution of, say, intolerance of uncertainty from general trait anxiety. The partial results are the more informative readout when the question is whether or which specific construct drives an association or if the effect is potentially driven by a transdiagnostic latent factor; the exploratory family is FDR-corrected.

At N = 32 the three primary hypotheses behave as follows. H2 (IU → belief_momentum) and H3 (IU → h_switch) reach one-sided significance uncorrected (p₁ ≈ 0.04 and ≈ 0.06) but do not survive within-family Holm; H1 (STICSA-T → noise_reactivity) is null at the bivariate level (r ≈ −0.19).

The instructive result is what the partial correlations reveal. Once the shared internalizing variance is removed, STICSA-T → noise_reactivity becomes the strongest single association in the table (partial r ≈ −0.37, p ≈ 0.04), i.e. the H1 effect is present but is masked at the bivariate level by IU-loaded shared variance. Within the exploratory regression grid, the inhibitory subscale of IU carries the strongest association with belief_momentum (β ≈ 0.43), more than the prospective subscale, which is theoretically coherent, since inhibitory IU (the action-paralysing facet) maps naturally onto reluctance to commit to a new state.

None of these survive multiplicity correction at the current N, and none should be reported as established. They are recorded here as the associations most likely to firm up toward the target N, and as a demonstration that the partial-correlation step changes which trait looks responsible for a given parameter association. So please take all of this with a grain of salt :)

Formally, we seek the posterior:p(\boldsymbol{\theta} \mid \mathbf{x}) \propto p(\mathbf{x} \mid \boldsymbol{\theta}) \cdot p(\boldsymbol{\theta})

where \boldsymbol{\theta} = (\text{pw}, \text{nr}, \text{bm}, h, \text{cs}, \text{pn}) \in \mathbb{R}^6 are the cognitive parameters (precision_weighting, noise_reactivity, belief_momentum, h_switch, cue_sensitivity, placement_noise) and \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^{54} is the feature vector. Rather than computing this posterior analytically or via sampling, we train a conditional density estimator q_\phi(\boldsymbol{\theta} \mid \mathbf{x}) parameterized by neural network weights \phi to approximate p(\boldsymbol{\theta} \mid \mathbf{x}) across the full joint space (\boldsymbol{\theta}, \mathbf{x}).

We approximated the posterior using neural posterior estimation (NPE) with learned summary statistics (

Radev et al., 2020), as implemented in the BayesFlow 2.0 framework for amortized Bayesian inference (

Radev et al., 2023a).

Specificially, the implemented inference pipeline uses the following architecture:



Figure 1:The Amortized Bayesian Inference Workflow.Agent Simulation → Feature Extraction → DeepSet(64) → FlowMatching → Posterior
     (CPU)            (deterministic)     (summary)    (inference)   (6 params)

Summary Network: A DeepSet (

Zaheer et al., 2017) maps the 54-dimensional feature vector (reshaped to a 1-element set) to a 64-dimensional summary representation. The DeepSet architecture is used (instead of an MLP) to comply with BayesFlow’s internal architecture requirements for condition passing.\mathbf{h} = \text{DeepSet}(\mathbf{x}) \in \mathbb{R}^{64}

Inference Network: FlowMatching (

Lipman et al., 2022; 

2024) with optimal transport and an MLP subnet (4 layers × 256 units, 5% dropout) learns a conditional normalizing flow from the 64-dimensional summary to the 6-dimensional posterior over parameters. FlowMatching was chosen over coupling flows for its faster convergence and better handling of multimodal posteriors.

How this works: the 64-dimensional summary \mathbf{h} conditions a Flow Matching model that learns a continuous normalizing flow from a standard normal base distribution to the conditional posterior:\boldsymbol{\theta} = F_\phi(\mathbf{z}; \mathbf{h}), \quad \mathbf{z} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I}_6)

The flow F_\phi is parameterized by an MLP with 4 hidden layers of 256 units each, 5% dropout, and mish activation. We use optimal transport coupling (

Tong et al., 2023) to improve training efficiency.

The total number of trainable parameters is approximately 850,000.

The network is trained on 100,000 simulated sessions:

Data generation. N_{\text{train}} = 100{,}000 simulations are generated in parallel. For each simulation:

Parameters \boldsymbol{\theta} are drawn from the uniform priors

A trial schedule is randomly selected from the 20 available schedules

The agent runs the full session, producing allocations \{\mathbf{g}_t\}

The 54-dimensional feature vector \mathbf{x} is extracted

The pre-generated feature vectors are then used to train the DeepSet + FlowMatching network:

Training. The network is trained offline (i.e., on the pre-generated dataset, not with on-the-fly simulation) for up to 300 epochs with:

Batch size: 256

Initial learning rate: 5 \times 10^{-4}

Optimizer: Adam (this is the default Keras settings)

Early stopping: patience 50, restoring best weights (monitored on validation loss)

Validation split: 10% (10,000 held-out simulations)

Loss function. BayesFlow’s default training objective for Flow Matching is the conditional flow matching loss (

Lipman et al., 2022; 

2024), which minimizes the expected squared error between the learned and target velocity fields:\mathcal{L}(\phi) = \mathbb{E}_{t, \boldsymbol{\theta}, \mathbf{z}, \mathbf{x}} \left[ \| v_\phi(t, \boldsymbol{\theta}_t; \mathbf{h}(\mathbf{x})) - u_t(\boldsymbol{\theta}_t \mid \boldsymbol{\theta}) \|^2 \right]

where t \sim \text{Uniform}(0, 1), \boldsymbol{\theta}_t = (1-t)\mathbf{z} + t\boldsymbol{\theta} (with optimal transport pairing), and u_t is the target velocity field.

How our loss curve looks like:



Figure 2:Training Loss and Validation Loss
To ensure both stability and validity of the inference pipeline, we run Simulation-Based Calibration (SBC) and Parameter Recoverability as complementary validation procedures.

Following 

Talts et al. (2018), we verify posterior calibration via SBC. For M = 500 simulations with known parameters the posterior is sampled and the rank of the true parameter within the posterior is computed. Specificially, this is how the procedure works:

Draw \boldsymbol{\theta}^* \sim p(\boldsymbol{\theta}) from the prior

Simulate data \mathbf{x}^* from the agent with \boldsymbol{\theta}^*

Draw K = 1000 posterior samples \{\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(k)}\}_{k=1}^K \sim q_\phi(\boldsymbol{\theta} \mid \mathbf{x}^*)

Compute the rank statistic: r_i = \sum_{k=1}^K \mathbb{I}[\theta_i^{(k)} < \theta_i^*] for each parameter i

Under correct posterior calibration, r_i \sim \text{Discrete Uniform}(0, K). Deviations from uniformity indicate systematic bias (mean \neq K/2) or miscalibration (variance \neq K^2/12).

Why we decided to take a feature-based approach

records.content:
Rather than feeding the raw 32-slot allocation time series to the neural network (which caused training instability due to sparsity, variable sequence lengths, and the curse of dimensionality), we extract a fixed-size vector of 54 behavioral summary statistics per session. This approach eliminates variable-length padding issues, replaces sparse integer inputs with continuous, bounded features, ensures identical feature computation for simulated and real participant data (no domain shift) and thus reduces the neural network’s task from “learn to extract behavioral patterns from raw sequences” to “learn to map extracted patterns to parameters” - which also best aligns with the core research focus.

Furthermore, this approach simplifies the integration of multimodal data while maintaining the same network architecture; and - even more interestingly - it potentially allows for generalization to various tasks rather than being limited to a single paradigm.

All 54 features satisfy the following requirements (to ensure traceability and computational stability):

Continuous and bounded: No discrete or unbounded values that could destabilize training

Deterministic: Given the same allocation sequence \{\mathbf{g}_t\} and schedule, the features are identical

Domain-invariant: The same extraction code operates on both simulated agent output and real participant data (to avoid preprocessing differences that could create domain shift)

Information-preserving: Each feature is designed to capture a specific aspect of behavior that distinguishes between parameter values, based on prior sensitivity analysis (see The inference agent, associated behavioral features in the parameter definition section)

1. mean_net_entropy — Mean Shannon entropy (base 2) of the net allocation over all trials: \bar{H} = \frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^T H(\mathbf{g}_t), where H(\mathbf{g}) = -\sum_s p_s \log_2 p_s and p_s = g_s / \sum_j g_j.

2. std_net_entropy — Standard deviation of per-trial entropy: \text{SD}(H(\mathbf{g}_1), \ldots, H(\mathbf{g}_T)).

3. mean_slots_occupied — Mean number of slots with \geq 1 net: \frac{1}{T} \sum_t |\{s : g_{t,s} > 0\}|.

4. mean_max_nets_slot — Mean maximum stacking depth: \frac{1}{T} \sum_t \max_s g_{t,s}.

5. frac_stacking — Fraction of trials where any slot has \geq 2 nets: \frac{1}{T} \sum_t \mathbb{I}[\max_s g_{t,s} \geq 2].

6. mean_circ_variance — Mean circular variance of the allocation: \bar{V} = \frac{1}{T} \sum_t (1 - R_t), where R_t = \|\sum_s p_s e^{i\phi_s}\| is the resultant length.

7. entropy_change_halves — Difference in mean entropy between the second and first halves of the session: \bar{H}_{t > T/2} - \bar{H}_{t \leq T/2}.

8. mean_angular_error — Mean unsigned angular distance (degrees) between the allocation circular mean and the actual outcome: \frac{1}{|\mathcal{O}|} \sum_{t \in \mathcal{O}} |\angle(\omega_t - \bar{\phi}_t^g)|, where \mathcal{O} is the set of outcome trials and \bar{\phi}_t^g is the circular mean of \mathbf{g}_t.

9. std_angular_error — Standard deviation of per-trial angular errors.

10. mean_defense_rate — Fraction of outcome trials where the attacked slot has \geq 1 net: \frac{1}{|\mathcal{O}|} \sum_{t \in \mathcal{O}} \mathbb{I}[g_{t, s(\omega_t)} > 0], where s(\omega) = \text{round}(\omega \cdot S / 2\pi) \mod S.

11. defense_rate_improvement — Defense rate in the last 3 episodes minus the first 3 episodes.

12. mean_tracking_error — Mean angular distance (degrees) between the allocation center on trial t and the previous outcome \omega_{t-1}. Measures how closely the agent tracks the most recent observation.

13. oddball_entropy_spike — Mean entropy on trial t+1 after an oddball, minus mean entropy on regular trials.

14. oddball_angular_shift — Mean angular shift (degrees) of allocation center from trial t-1 to t+1 around oddball trials.

15. oddball_angular_shift_regular — Same metric computed around non-oddball outcome trials (baseline).

16. oddball_shift_ratio — Feature 14 divided by Feature 15. Values > 1 indicate the agent reacts more strongly to oddballs than to regular outcomes.

17. oddball_recovery_speed — Mean angular distance of allocation center on trials t+1, t+2, t+3 from the pre-oddball position (t-1), averaged across oddballs.

18. frac_oddball_followed — Fraction of oddballs where the allocation on t+1 is closer to the oddball direction \omega_t than the allocation on t-1 was.

22. transition_recovery_slope — Linear regression slope of angular error over trials 1–5 after transitions. Negative slope = error decreasing = fast recovery.

23. transition_entropy_peak — Maximum entropy in the first 3 post-transition trials.

24. transition_entropy_recovery — Number of trials until entropy returns to baseline (\leq \bar{H} + 0.5 \cdot \text{SD}(H)) after a transition.

25. mean_angular_error_late_episode — Mean angular error on trials 6+ within each episode (baseline accuracy after initial learning).

26. transition_recovery_improvement — Linear slope of recovery speeds across the 8 transitions. Positive = recovery gets faster over the session (meta-learning).

In an initial fit with the h_switch prior extended to [0.005, 0.35], a large
share of participants had posteriors pressed against the upper bound: 59% had
their 97.5% credible limit pinned at 0.35, and 68% had posterior means above
0.30. Taken at face value this would imply that most participants believe the
latent state switches on roughly every third trial — far more often than the
true switch rate (~0.05 per trial; episodes are 16–24 trials long). This was
implausible on its face and motivated a systematic investigation rather than

records.content:
In the v2 agent, a single oddball produces an outcome at the other latent
state’s location (the oddball displacement of +120° coincides with the
alternative state). Working through the Bayesian belief update with a
freshly-committed prior, the raw posterior over the alternative state crosses
0.5 — i.e. the agent commits to a full state switch — exactly whenh_{\text{switch}} > \rho_{\text{eff}} = \rho_{\text{fixed}} \cdot \text{noise\_reactivity},

with \rho_{\text{fixed}} = 0.10. This is the Piray & Daw (2021)
volatility-versus-stochasticity trade-off emerging directly from the mixture
likelihood: whether a surprising outcome is attributed to a changed rule
(volatility, h_switch) or to noise (stochasticity, noise_reactivity).

The crucial consequence is that the switching behaviour is governed by whether
the agent is above or below this threshold, not by the precise value of
h_switch. Once h_switch exceeds 0.1 · noise_reactivity, the agent switches
at essentially every oddball, and there are no further switching opportunities
to exploit. Behaviour therefore saturates: higher h_switch values become
behaviourally indistinguishable.



Figure 1:Switch-interpretation behaviour (oddball_follow_switch) as a function of
h_switch at four noise_reactivity levels. Each curve rises sharply at its
own threshold h = 0.1 \cdot nr (dotted vertical lines) and then plateaus.
Above threshold, behaviour is flat — h_switch is no longer identifiable from
behaviour. The highest informative region is reached at h \approx 0.30, the
threshold for the largest noise_reactivity in the prior (nr = 3.0).

Because noise_reactivity ranges up to 3.0, the largest informative value of
h_switch is approximately 0.10 \cdot 3.0 = 0.30. Beyond this, no
noise_reactivity value leaves the behaviour unsaturated, so additional prior
mass above 0.30 contributes only non-identifiable parameter space — precisely
the region that produces the ceiling artefact.

principled criterion is the saturation analysis, not the raw correlation. Both
converge on the same conclusion.

Decision: the h_switch prior upper bound is set to 0.30, the point at
which the switch threshold for the maximum noise_reactivity is reached. This
is the largest bound for which the entire prior remains behaviourally
identifiable, and it avoids the implausible near-ceiling values while preserving
the joint recovery of h_switch and noise_reactivity.

records.content:
Across participants, posterior h_switch and noise_reactivity are positively
correlated (r = +0.60). This is theoretically expected: a person who perceives
the environment as more volatile (high h_switch) and simultaneously attributes
surprising outcomes more readily to genuine change rather than noise is
expressing a coherent, correlated cognitive style. Because the two parameters
sit on either side of the same switch threshold, a positive association across
individuals is exactly what the volatility/stochasticity framework predicts.

A coupling of this kind could, in principle, also arise as an inference
artefact — if the network compressed the two parameters along the threshold
line. We tested this directly. In simulation, noise_reactivity and h_switch
were drawn independently; if the inference induced a spurious coupling, the
estimated parameters would correlate despite the independent ground truth.
They do not: the estimated correlation is ≈ 0 (and slightly negative), while the
real-participant correlation is strongly positive.



Figure 3:Left: simulated data with noise_reactivity and h_switch drawn
independently. The estimated parameters show no spurious correlation
(estimated r ≈ 0), confirming the inference does not manufacture coupling.
Right: real participants. The posteriors show a clear positive coupling
(r = +0.60), and all participants lie above the single-oddball switch threshold
h = 0.1 \cdot nr (dashed line) — i.e. they reliably treat oddballs as state
switches. The coupling is therefore a genuine psychological effect.

Because the simulated check rules out an inference-induced artefact, the
correlation observed in the real data reflects genuine individual differences in
cognitive style. This is a substantive finding rather than a nuisance, and it is
consistent with the prior theoretical expectation that perceived volatility and
the propensity to attribute change (rather than noise) covary.

records.content:
This chapter describes the computational modeling pipeline used to estimate participant-specific cognitive parameters from behavioral data. The pipeline combines three components:

The inference agent - a parametric belief-update model that maps cognitive parameters to observable behavior

A feature extraction module - deterministic extraction of 40 behavioral summary statistics from net allocations

An amortized Bayesian inference network - a neural density estimator (BayesFlow) that inverts the agent model, mapping observed behavioral features to posterior distributions over cognitive parameters

The key advantage of this methodological approach is that inference is amortized. Specificially, a neural network is trained once on a large corpus of simulated agent–environment interactions, after which posterior estimation for any real participant takes approximately 3 seconds. This enables full Bayesian uncertainty quantification without the computational cost of traditional MCMC methods.

Further information about Amortized Bayesian Inference and BayesFlow 2.0 can be found here (insert Radev et al., 2023 and website link)

records.content:
Participants in the TAMBI mosquito defense task face a complex learning problem: they must infer hidden environmental regularities - latent state transitions, cue-dependent directional offsets, and the distinction between noise and genuine change - from noisy, intermittent outcome feedback. Not all participants approach this problem in the same way. Some may engage in sophisticated latent structure inference, tracking hidden states and attributing surprises to their appropriate sources. Others may rely on simpler strategies: following the most recent outcome direction, or learning the association between cue colours and attack directions without ever building a model of the latent state dynamics. A small number may not engage meaningfully at all.

Before we can interpret the cognitive parameters estimated by our inference agent (

Amortized Bayesian Inference), we need to establish which type of learning strategy each participant is using. This is essential for three reasons:

Validity of parameter estimates. The four cognitive parameters (precision weighting, noise reactivity, belief momentum, perceived volatility) are defined within a latent-structure-learning agent. Estimating these parameters for a participant who is not performing structure learning would be scientifically inappropriate (analogous to fitting a linear regression model to non-linear data)

Participant exclusion. Participants who clicked randomly or without meaningful engagement should be identified and excluded from subsequent analyses. Here, model comparison provides an objective, data-driven exclusion criterion.

Characterisation of the learning strategy spectrum. The distribution of winning models across participants provides insight into the prevalence of different learning strategies in the sample, and can be related to instruction condition and trait-level measures.

records.content:
We employ BayesFlow’s ModelComparisonApproximator (Radev et al., 2023; Schmitt et al., 2023) to perform amortized Bayesian model comparison. The approach follows the same simulation-based inference logic as the parameter estimation pipeline: a neural classifier is trained on a large corpus of simulated behavioral data (generated from all candidate models), and then applied to real participant data to estimate posterior model probabilities.

The key advantage over traditional model comparison methods (e.g., BIC, AIC, Bayes factors via bridge sampling) is that amortized model comparison:

Operates on the same 40 behavioral summary features used for parameter estimation (ensuring consistency)

Provides well-calibrated posterior probabilities over models (not just point estimates or ranking)

Requires no per-participant optimization or sampling at inference time (~1 ms per participant)

Can be validated via confusion matrices, calibration curves, and model recovery analyses before application to real data

records.content:
Rather than comparing a large number of models that differ in subtle ways, we define a compact set of five models that span the qualitative spectrum from disengaged behavior to full latent structure inference. This design reflects a principled ablation logic: each successive model adds a qualitatively distinct cognitive capability.



Figure 1:The five models.

The rationale for limiting the set to these five models is twofold. First, the cognitive transitions they span (no learning → outcome tracking → cue association → multi-location coverage → latent structure inference) capture the most important qualitative distinctions in learning strategy. Second, model variants that differ only in continuous parameter settings within the structure-learning agent (e.g. with or without oddball attribution, with fixed or free volatility) are better handled by the parameter estimation pipeline, where these differences manifest as different parameter values rather than as discrete model classes. Maintaining them as separate models would constitute “double dipping” - testing the same cognitive dimension at both the model and parameter level.

The one model added beyond the original four, M_STRUCT4, deserves a word of justification because it does not introduce a new capability so much as a distinct interpretation of the task. A participant who has noticed that each cue is attacked from two structured directions could respond in two very different ways: by inferring which of the two hidden states is currently active and committing to it (M_STRUCT), or by simply covering both directions for each cue at once and never bothering to infer the current state (M_STRUCT4). Both look structured, and both are clearly distinct from single-direction tracking, but only the first is genuine latent-state inference. Without M_STRUCT4 in the set, a participant using the permanent-hedging strategy would be misassigned to M_STRUCT and counted, wrongly, as a structure-inferring learner. M_STRUCT4 exists precisely to absorb those participants and protect the interpretation of an M_STRUCT classification.

Purpose: Tests whether behavior can be explained by simple exponential moving average (EMA) tracking of the most recent outcome direction, without any cue differentiation or latent state inference.

Mechanism: The agent maintains a single direction estimate \hat{\mu} that is updated after each observed outcome \omega_t via a circular EMA:\hat{\mu} \leftarrow \left(\hat{\mu} + \alpha \cdot \angle(\omega_t - \hat{\mu})\right) \mod 2\pi

where \alpha is the learning rate and \angle(\cdot) denotes the signed angular distance in [-\pi, \pi]. The agent does not distinguish between cue colours: outcomes from both Cue A and Cue B update the same direction estimate \hat{\mu}. Net allocation uses the same power-sharpening mechanism as the full agent:g_s = \text{round}\left(\frac{[\text{vM}(\phi_s; \hat{\mu}, \kappa_{\text{eff}})]^{1+\text{pw}}}{\sum_j [\text{vM}(\phi_j; \hat{\mu}, \kappa_{\text{eff}})]^{1+\text{pw}}} \cdot 7\right)

where \kappa_{\text{eff}} = \kappa_{\text{fixed}} \cdot \text{pw}.

Free parameters:

Parameter

Range

Description

precision_weighting

[0.1, 5.0]

Controls allocation concentration (same as M_STRUCT)

\alpha

[0.01, 0.5]

EMA learning rate

What this model cannot capture: Cue-specific behaviour (different placements for Cue A vs. Cue B), latent state transitions (sudden direction changes), or oddball attribution.

records.content:
Purpose: Tests whether behaviour can be explained by trial-by-trial tracking with learned cue-colour associations. This represents a form of associative learning that does not require inferring hidden states.

Mechanism: Identical to M_TRACK_SIMPLE, but with the addition of a cue-specific angular offset \hat{\delta}_B that is learned online:

For Cue A: prediction at \hat{\mu}_A

For Cue B: prediction at (\hat{\mu}_A + \hat{\delta}_B) \mod 2\pi

When a Cue B outcome is observed, both the base direction \hat{\mu}_A and the offset \hat{\delta}_B are updated with different learning rates:\hat{\delta}_B \leftarrow (\hat{\delta}_B + \alpha \cdot 0.3 \cdot \text{PE}_B) \mod 2\pi\hat{\mu}_A \leftarrow (\hat{\mu}_A + \alpha \cdot 0.7 \cdot \text{PE}_B) \mod 2\pi

where \text{PE}_B = \angle(\omega_t - [\hat{\mu}_A + \hat{\delta}_B]).

Free parameters: Same as M_TRACK_SIMPLE (precision_weighting, \alpha). The offset \hat{\delta}_B is a learned internal state, not a prior parameter.

What this model adds over M_TRACK_SIMPLE: The ability to place nets at different angular positions depending on the cue colour - a directly observable regularity in the task.

What this model cannot capture: Latent state transitions (the agent has no concept of alternating hidden states), oddball attribution (all surprises are treated as signal), or episode-boundary adaptation.

Purpose: The primary model. Tests whether behaviour reflects latent structure inference - tracking hidden states, attributing surprises to oddball noise versus genuine change, and adapting beliefs after state transitions.

Mechanism: The full reduced-form inference agent as described in the Parameter Estimation chapter. Implements a two-state Hidden Markov Model with cue-dependent offsets, oddball mixture observation model, and belief momentum.

The list and priors are imported directly from reduced_agent_v3, so the model-comparison agent and the parameter-estimation agent are guaranteed to be the same generative process. See the Parameter Estimation chapter for the complete specification.

What this model adds over M_TRACK_CUE: The concept of latent states (z \in \{0,1\}) that transition with probability h, producing systematic direction changes that the agent can anticipate. The oddball mixture that allows the agent to separate noise from signal. The belief momentum that captures individual differences in adaptation speed. The two additional parameters that complete the v3 agent - cue_sensitivity (how fully the cue-colour offset is learned) and placement_noise (undirected action-level scatter) - are along for the ride here rather than central to the comparison: they refine how the structured allocation is produced, not whether the participant is inferring structure, which is the question the model comparison asks.

records.content:
Purpose: Distinguishes genuine latent-state inference from a structurally-aware but non-inferential strategy. This is the model that separates a participant who infers and commits to the current hidden state from one who merely covers all the structured locations at once.

Mechanism: The participant has discovered that each cue is associated with two structured attack directions - the two rotational positions of the hidden state - but does not infer which state is currently active. Instead of running a two-state HMM and committing to the inferred state, they permanently hedge fifty-fifty across both rotational modes for the current cue. Because the cues alternate, all four structured locations (two cues times two modes) remain continuously active across the session. Concretely, the model maintains up to two direction modes per cue via circular online k-means: each new outcome is assigned to its nearest existing mode and nudged toward it at rate \alpha, and if it falls more than a separation threshold (≈50°) away from all existing modes while a slot is free, it spawns the second mode. The action is then a fifty-fifty von-Mises mixture over the current cue’s available modes, with no state belief and no temporal weighting.

Free parameters:

Parameter

Range

Description

precision_weighting

[0.1, 5.0]

Controls allocation concentration

\alpha

[0.01, 0.5]

circular EMA learning rate for the modes

The two free parameters are deliberately parallel to the tracker models, so that M_STRUCT4 is not advantaged by extra flexibility when it is compared against them.

What this model adds over M_TRACK_CUE: the ability to represent two structured directions per cue simultaneously, rather than a single tracked direction. M_TRACK_CUE collapses each cue onto one direction and cannot hold both rotational positions at once.

What distinguishes it from M_STRUCT: M_STRUCT4 never commits to a current state and never tracks transitions over time. Instead, it treats the task as a static four-location coverage problem; M_STRUCT treats it as a dynamic two-state inference problem. This is exactly the behavioural signature of the “permanent hedging” responders seen in the 

Oddball-Response Diagnostics, and giving that strategy its own model is what stops it from contaminating the M_STRUCT class.

records.content:
The model comparison uses BayesFlow 2.0’s ModelComparisonApproximator, which implements amortized Bayesian model comparison via a neural classifier trained on simulated data from all candidate models.

The architecture consists of:

Adapter: Renames the model index to inference_variables, applies one-hot encoding (\mathbb{R}^1 \to \mathbb{R}^4), and converts to float32.

Summary Network: A DeepSet (Zaheer et al., 2017) with summary_dim=8 and depth=1 processes the feature vector (reshaped to a 1-element set). The DeepSet maps the 40-dimensional feature vector to an 8-dimensional embedding.

Classifier Network: An MLP with two hidden layers of 64 units each (SiLU activation, no dropout) maps the 8-dimensional embedding to 4 logits, which are passed through a softmax to produce posterior model probabilities.

The total number of trainable parameters is approximately 8,000 (which is quite small - this is intentional and allows to prevent overfitting, given the relatively low complexity of the 4-class classification problem).

Data generation. N = 40{,}000 simulations are generated in parallel (10,000 per model, balanced). For each simulation:

A model is selected uniformly at random from {M_RANDOM, M_TRACK_SIMPLE, M_TRACK_CUE, M_STRUCT4, M_STRUCT}

Parameters are drawn from the model’s prior

A trial schedule is randomly selected from the 20 available schedules

The model simulates the full session

The 54-feature vector is extracted

Class balance is maintained by uniform model sampling during generation.

Training. The classifier is trained via cross-entropy loss for 200 epochs with:

Batch size: 512

Cosine learning rate decay: 10^{-4} \to 10^{-6}

Train/validation split: 90%/10%

No early stopping (the small network converges quickly and does not overfit)

Loss function. The standard categorical cross-entropy:\mathcal{L} = -\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \sum_{m=1}^{4} y_{i,m} \log \hat{p}_{i,m}

where y_{i,m} is the one-hot encoded true model index and \hat{p}_{i,m} is the predicted probability for model m.

records.content:
For each model, we compute a reliability diagram, showing the relationship between the classifier’s predicted probability (confidence) and the empirical frequency of correct classification. A well-calibrated classifier has predicted probability equal to empirical accuracy across all confidence levels.

The Expected Calibration Error (ECE) quantifies the deviation from perfect calibration:\text{ECE} = \sum_{b=1}^{B} \frac{n_b}{N} \left| \text{acc}(b) - \text{conf}(b) \right|

where the confidence range [0, 1] is partitioned into B = 10 bins, n_b is the number of samples in bin b, and \text{acc}(b) and \text{conf}(b) are the mean accuracy and confidence within that bin.

Target: ECE < 0.05 for all models (i.e., predicted probabilities are reliable).

For each model: when data were generated from that model, what is the distribution of posterior probability assigned to the true model? This is the model-comparison analogue of Simulation-Based Calibration (Talts et al., 2018): if the classifier is well-calibrated, the distribution of p(\text{true model} \mid \text{data}) should be concentrated near 1.0 for unambiguous cases and spread toward 0.5 for cases where two models produce similar behaviour (e.g., M_TRACK_SIMPLE with high learning rate and M_TRACK_CUE with near-zero \hat{\delta}_B).

We report:

Mean p(\text{true}): The average posterior probability assigned to the generating model. Higher = better discrimination.

Fraction correct (p > 0.5): How often the true model has the highest probability. This equals the per-model accuracy from the confusion matrix.

Fraction confident (p > 0.8): How often the classifier is highly confident about the correct model. This measures the strength of the behavioral signatures.

records.content:
This section documents how participants respond to oddball outcomes - the behaviour that the noise_reactivity (nr) parameter is designed to capture - and explains, on the basis of that behaviour, why the nr signal is intrinsically weak in the current paradigm. The analysis aims a fine-grained characterization of participant behaviour
in the present data. It is fully reproducible via oddball_diagnostics.py.

hierarchy.lvl1: Oddball-Response Diagnostics and the Weak noise_reactivity Signal
Oddball-Response Diagnostics and the Weak noise_reactivity Signal

records.content: noise_reactivity is the parameter on the stochasticity side of the Piray & Daw (2021) volatility-versus-stochasticity trade-off: it governs whether a surprising oddball outcome is attributed to noise (the rule is unchanged) or to a genuine state change. In parameter recovery it is consistently the weakest of the six parameters (BayesFlow correlation ≈ 0.63, against ≥ 0.82 for every other parameter), with a classic  regression-to-the-mean error profile. Before accepting this as an irreducible property, we characterised the underlying behaviour directly, i.e. what do participants actually do after an oddball, how informative are those events, and what about the task structure limits the signal.

records.content:
On an oddball trial the observed attack location (actual_vector_angle) sits approximately 120° away from the nominal state (target_vector_angle); the oddball displacement of +120° coincides with the other latent state for that cue. On regular trials the same difference is only the von-Mises sensory noise (≈ 8°). The behaviourally meaningful references for the next same-cue placement are therefore:

STAY is defined as placement near the nominal state (target_vector_angle of the   oddball trial), i.e. the participant treats the oddball as noise (high nr)

FOLLOW is defined as placement near the displaced attack location   (actual_vector_angle), i.e. the  participant treats the oddball as a state switch (low nr).

Note

The oddball location must be referenced to actual_vector_angle, not target_vector_angle. Using the target collapses STAY and FOLLOW onto the same point and makes the classification meaningless. The feature-extraction pipeline and the agent both use actual_vector_angle throughout; this was verified end-to-end (see the agent and feature-extraction sections).

records.content: Across 536 clean oddball events (those with valid same-cue placements both before and after the oddball) from 34 participants, the next same-cue placement moves on average 61.9° relative to the pre-oddball placement, with a mean signed move of +25.6° toward the oddball location. This net movement is modest: participants do not, on average, chase the displaced outcome, but neither do they fully ignore it.

records.content:
Two structural features of the data combine to limit nr identifiability:

Few clean informative events per participant. Oddballs are rare (≈ 10% of trials), giving a median of 16 clean events per participant (range 10–18). With roughly a third of those being uninformative hedges, only about ten clean stay-versus-follow decisions remain per participant from which to estimate nr.

A third of the behaviour is off-axis. The nr mechanism maps onto a binary stay/follow axis, but 34% of responses are diffuse or hedged. This off-axis behaviour is partly absorbed by placement_noise (action-level scatter) and does not inform nr, so the effective signal is smaller than the raw event count suggests.

Together these explain the flat, distributed feature-importance profile observed for nr (no single behavioural feature dominates) and the regression-to-the-mean recovery: with little per-participant information, the posterior is pulled toward the prior mean except for participants with unusually consistent stay or follow behaviour. So this is an intrinsic property of the paradigm and not an implementation issue. The agent and feature pipeline reproduce nr-dependent following in the correct direction (the simulated follow rate decreases monotonically with nr).

records.content:
noise_reactivity should be reported with its posterior uncertainty rather than as a precise point estimate. However, its calibration is sound (clean SBC) and the posteriors are honest; the limited signal manifests as appropriately wide posteriors (not as miscalibration).

Additionally, the three-way response structure (stay / follow / hedge) is itself a substantive behavioural description and can be reported as a model-agnostic characterisation of how participants treat surprising outcomes.

Downstream individual-difference analyses involving nr should weight by posterior uncertainty and check robustness to the small number of low-nr participants who anchor the low end of the distribution (working on it)

This section documents the posterior predictive checks (PPCs) that drove the
development of the inference agent from its five-parameter form to the final
six-parameter version. I’d like to guide you through why a misspecification was
suspected, how it was diagnosed, what change resolved it, and exactly how well
the final model reproduces participant behaviour, including the residual
discrepancies that remain by design. All checks are reproducible via
posterior_predictive_checks.py.

Parameter recovery and simulation-based calibration establish that the inference network inverts the agent correctly. They do not establish that the agent reproduces real behaviour. A posterior predictive check closes this gap: for each participant we draw parameter sets from the posterior, simulate the agent on that participant’s exact trial schedule, extract the same behavioural features from the simulated and the observed data, and ask whether the observed feature value falls within the simulated posterior-predictive interval. A feature whose observed value lies above the 95% predictive interval signals that the agent cannot produce enough of that behaviour - a misspecification.

The checks focus on a panel of “switchiness” features that capture how sharply
and how often participants change their net placement, since this turned out to be the most critical part. Specificially, the features are the spontaneous switch rate, the fraction of large trial-to-trial shifts, the mean trial shift, belief lability, the oddball-following measures, and the within-state placement variability. These are the behaviours most diagnostic of the inference-level and action-level parameters.

In the five-parameter agent (deterministic belief-to-action mapping), the PPCs revealed a systematic and pervasive failure, namely that across participants, essentially every switchiness feature fell above the 95% predictive interval. The agent was uniformly too stable - it could not reproduce the trial-to-trial variability participants actually show. A representative diagnosis traced a systematic bias of approximately 27° in switchy/oddball-shift features.

Crucially, this was not a failure of the inference step (recovery and SBC were clean) but of the generative model: with a deterministic mapping from belief to action, the agent placed its nets at exactly the predictive mean on every trial, whereas participants still scatter their placements around it over trials.

Before adding any parameter, the source of the excess variability was localised through a structured set of diagnostics, ruling out alternatives in turn:

Not cue contamination. The switchy features were re-derived with cue-correction (comparing each post-event placement to the nearest same-cue trial), and the misspecification persisted.

Not a timing or indexing error. The action-then-outcome ordering was verified: the allocation on each trial is chosen on the belief before the outcome is observed, and the oddball reaction appears earliest on the following trial, as expected.

Not structured inference. The excess scatter was shown to be undirected and memoryless: the lag-1 autocorrelation of within-state deviations from the local mean is ≈ 0 for the tested participants (+0.03) and a pure jitter process, and the scatter is not explained by the κ noise (≈ 8°, i.e. spread over up to three slots), which is far smaller than the observed within-state variability (≈ 32°).

The residual was therefore identified as within-state placement stochasticity: undirected, memoryless scatter in the belief-to-action mapping, present even when the latent belief is stable (to be discussed - I called it “stable belief” since it is not explainable by any other relationship to other metrics. However, it could be an alternative expression of belief uncertainty too - an alternative strategy instead of spreading the nets over more slots in each single trial).

A single sixth parameter, placement_noise, was added to capture this scatter (see The Inference Agent). It applies a zero-mean circular Gaussian jitter to the predictive distribution before net placement, leaving the structured inference deterministic. Setting placement_noise to zero recovers the five-parameter agent exactly.

This was a deliberate, minimal intervention. The agent’s complexity was not increased further: the structured large jumps that some participants make (template-style re-inference - this is something to investigate with a hypothesis-set agent architecture) are deliberately left unmodelled, and placement_noise captures only the undirected within-state scatter, which the diagnostics showed to be the dominant source of the misspecification.

With placement_noise free, the PPCs improve dramatically. hierarchy.lvl2: The two residuals, and why they remain by design
The two residuals, and why they remain by design

records.content:
Two features remain systematically above the interval, and both point to the same deliberately-unmodelled phenomenon:

belief_lability (21% inside, 27 of 34 above, mean exceedance ≈ 8°): the observed mean is ≈ 46° against a predictive median of ≈ 34°.

oddball_shift_ratio / oddball_angular_shift (47% / 59% inside): the observed oddball-driven shift exceeds the predictive median (for oddball_angular_shift, mean exceedance ≈ 15°).

These features capture the large, structured jumps that participants make on a minority of oddball trials, which are the template-style re-inference in which a participant, on encountering a surprising outcome, jumps a full ~120° to the alternative state. The agent reproduces undirected scatter (placement_noise) and threshold-based state switching (h_switch / noise_reactivity), but it does not model this large-jump re-inference, which accounts for roughly the top quarter of large shifts. belief_lability is the feature most sensitive to exactly these jumps, which is why it is the hardest residual.

This is a documented modelling boundary rather than an unexplained failure. The oddball-response diagnostics show that a third of post-oddball responses are diffuse or hedged rather than clean stays or follows (see
Oddball-Response Diagnostics), and the structured large jumps sit at the far end of that distribution. Capturing them would require an additional mechanism; the decision was made to keep the agent minimal and report the large-jump behaviour as a limitation.

The within-state placement marker shows a smaller residual (59% inside, mean exceedance ≈ 4° among the 13 above): the participant placement distribution is bimodal (mostly very stable, occasionally large jumps), whereas the Gaussian
jitter is unimodal. The mean amount of scatter matches, but the shape differs - the same total variability arrives as continuous medium scatter in the agent versus sharp bands plus occasional jumps in participants. This is the action-level counterpart of the same structured-jump phenomenon.

One participant, VP 5272 - an extreme cue-blind outlier with very high noise_reactivity - remains above the interval on all nine features. This single participant is broadly more switchy than the model across the board and is flagged as an outlier rather than driving model changes.

The posterior predictive checks justify the six-parameter model on behavioural grounds: the five-parameter agent was misspecified (too stable), the excess variability was diagnosed as undirected within-state placement scatter, and a single action-level parameter resolves the misspecification for the large majority of features while remaining cleanly identifiable. The residuals are confined to features that index a specific, deliberately-unmodelled behaviour
(large structured re-inference jumps), which is reported transparently as a boundary of the current model rather than concealed.
