records.content:
M5 on continuous \lvert I_e \rvert confounds three things: (i) genuine cross-cue inference, (ii) placement noise, and (iii) cue confusion (the placement might happen to be near the new c_2 target by virtue of being near the old c_1 target). M5b isolates (i) cleanly by reducing the DV to a binary comparison that is invariant to (ii) and that explicitly contrasts (i) against (iii).
However, M5 and M5b are still formally complementary because M5b tests whether cross-cue inference is happening at all while M5 tests how close to “perfect” it is when it is happening.

Why a seperate classification in rule-appliers vs naive participants?

Because we want to understand whether participants identify the rules even if we do not tell them what (exactly) is going on (condition 1 and 2) and how long it takes them to do so. Furthermore, also participants that are informed about the rules (condition 3) might forget, misunderstand, discard or simply ignore the rules.

The cue-dissociation analyses (M5b plus the floor diagnostic) reveal substantial inter-individual heterogeneity in how participants engage rule 2. To make this heterogeneity tractable, the pipeline includes a per-participant classification step that sorts participants into rule-application classes based on their cue-dissociation behaviour.

A participant’s behaviour is summarised by their per-episode cue-dissociation rate, computed separately for two episode subsets:

Early episodes: episodes 1-3 (the period in which a participant could still be constructing the structural model from data).

Late episodes: episodes 4-8 (after the participant has had time to learn).

Four classes are defined:

Immediate applier: cue-dissociation rate > 0.6 in both early and late subsets. The participant is engaging the rule from session start.

Late applier: cue-dissociation rate > 0.6 in late episodes but \leq 0.6 in early episodes. The participant discovered the rule mid-session.

Non-applier: cue-dissociation rate < 0.5 in late episodes. Worse than chance, even after the full session.

Ambiguous: anything else (e.g., 0.5 \leq rate \leq 0.6 in late episodes).

The 0.6 threshold is above chance (random placement yields ~50% cue-dissociation by construction); the 0.5 floor for non-applier ensures the participant is not just near chance.

For each participant in the immediate or late applier class, the discovery episode is the smallest episode index at which a 2-episode moving window of cue-dissociation crosses 0.6. For immediate appliers, this is 1 by definition; for late appliers, it is the mid-session episode at which the rule is first reliably applied. The distribution of discovery episodes by condition is a temporal signature of when participants figure out (or apply) the structural rule, which is itself theoretically interesting (and connects to mental-health-linked individual differences as a downstream analysis; follows soon).

Why check for anticipatory behavior?

Because we want to check whether participants adjust their net placement to the new latent state even if they are still in the old one. This would be a signature of latent state inference.

A question raised during pilot analysis was whether some participants (mainly condition 3) anticipate transitions before they occur, by drifting their placements toward the new expected target in the last few trials of the old episode.

The plot_pre_transition_anticipation routine produces a two-panel figure on the 5 trials immediately preceding each transition.

Panel A - Anticipatory drift toward the next target: signed angular displacement from the old target, projected onto the direction of the upcoming shift. Positive values mean placements drift toward the new target before it is revealed. Different conditions are plotted as separate trajectories. If condition 3 anticipates, this curve should be positive and rising as the transition approaches; if not, it should be flat at zero.

Panel B - Pre-transition error trajectory: per-condition mean \lvert e_t \rvert over the same 5-trial window. If condition 3 participants anticipate, pre-transition error should rise in C3 as the transition approaches (because they are drifting away from the old target).

At the current N, the results do not support the idea that participants anticipate the latent state transitions (C3 has lower pre-transition error throughout the window but does not show systematic drift toward the next target). However, this analysis will also be applied to the rule-appliers (that will become informative at greater N though) based on the observations described in the sections above.

Why another transition reactivity check?

Because this provides a control mechanism for the interpretation of the M2 effects.

M2 measures post-transition recovery using raw \lvert e_t \rvert, which conflates two things: how much was the participant perturbed by the transition, and how good was their placement before the transition. A participant who was tightly placed before the transition is necessarily more perturbed by it (because the new target is \sim 120° away from their old position), while a participant whose placement was already noisy will appear less perturbed.

To control for this, the pipeline includes a baseline-normalised recovery visualisation.

For each transition, the pre-transition baseline is computed as the mean \lvert e_t \rvert over the 3 trials immediately before the transition (in the old episode). The recovery trajectory \lvert e_t \rvert / \text{baseline} is then plotted over the 5 trials following the transition.

A ratio of 1.0 means current error equals the pre-transition baseline; a ratio of 2.0 means error has doubled; a ratio below 1.0 means error is even smaller than baseline (which can happen after a successful reorientation if the participants new-state placement is more accurate than their old-state one).

recovery_relative_to_baseline.png includes to panels showing (A) the recovery ratio trajectory by condition, and (B) the per-participant “peak ratio” (= the largest perturbation each participant experienced relative to their baseline) by condition. Panel B is thus a condition-level summary of relative transition disruption.



This diagnostic clarifies whether condition differences in post-transition recovery are about speed of reorientation (which should manifest as condition differences in the ratio trajectory) or about baseline placement quality (which should show no condition difference in the ratio after the first 1-2 trials).

Does instruction help them place their nets faster, and are they showing meta-learning of the episode structure?

                + tau + episode_index_c + episode_length_c

A positive coefficient means: late in the experiment, the within-episode speedup is less steep than early, because participants are already fast at episode start. Direct behavioural evidence of meta-learning of episode structure)

Did they win? Does the participant actually block the mosquito?

Dependent variable. defense_rate ∈ {0, 1} (whether the mosquito was blocked, on each trial with a delivered outcome (oddball trials excluded))

records.content:
We assume that the first ~15-30 trials of each participant’s session might be qualitatively different from the rest of the session for several specific theoretical reasons. For condition 3 participants (rules explained), the early trials are simply the first chance to apply the generative model they entered the experiment with - to data that, from their perspective, has the structure they were told it has. For conditions 1 and 2 (basic / rules-mentioned), the same trials are when participants are constructing their generative model from scratch, e.g. they don’t yet know there are two cues with different distributions, they don’t yet know about the alternating latent state, they don’t yet know which trials are noise to be discounted.

The strongest theoretical prediction of the instruction manipulation is therefore not (only) that condition 3 participants are better on average over the whole session,- it is that they are better earlier, because they enter with a model that condition 1/2 participants must construct from data. By the end of the session, the conditions may have (partially) converged. That is, condition 1 having figured out the structure from evidence, condition 3 having applied it all along. The condition main effects in the full-session models are then a mixture of “early differences where the manipulation matters” and “late convergence where it does not”, which might partially dilute the manipulation signature (even if interaction effects with the trial/episode index are included, the effect decreases over the experiment as soon as condition 1/2 participants catch up). And the early-phase companion analyses target this head-on by restricting the sample to the early trials and using trial_index (centred within the early-phase sample) as a learning-curve predictor.

These analyses are conceptually (partially) adjacent to M5 in 

Primary GLMMs (both ask “when does behaviour change relative to ground truth?”) but they use entirely different statistical machinery and rest on different operationalisations. Again, the aim is to provide convergent evidence (a finding that emerges both under the parametric M5 specification and under at least one of the non-parametric / semi-parametric alternatives is much more credible than any alone).

The two analyses are:

Change-point analysis (M_CP) (Layer 5A), which is an offline change-point detection algorithm that is run per participant on the trial-by-trial trajectory. Detected change-points are compared to the true episode episode boundaries.

Time-to-recovery survival analysis (M_SURV) (Layer 5B). Here, for each true transition, the number of trials elapsed until the participant’s net mean falls within a tolerance window of the new target (episode mean for the respective color cue) is treated as a time-to-event outcome with right censoring.

Both are implemented in temporal_dynamics_analysis.py.

For each participant, the per-trial signal is the signed angular distance of the participant’s net mean from a per-participant reference angle (signed difference is wrapped to get the euclidean distance instead of circular one).

We use Pruned Exact Linear Time (PELT) segmentation (Killick, Fearnhead, & Eckley, 2012) implemented in the ruptures Python library (Truong, Oudre, & Vayatis, 2020). PELT minimises a penalised cost function\sum_{k=1}^{K+1} \mathcal{C}\!\big(s_{t_{k-1}+1:t_k}\big) + \beta \cdot K,

over all possible numbers (K) and locations (t_1, \ldots, t_K) of change-points, where \mathcal{C} is a per-segment cost function and \beta is the penalty per added change-point. PELT solves this exactly in \mathcal{O}(n) amortised time under mild conditions (Killick et al., 2012), via dynamic programming with a pruning rule that discards dominated candidate change-points. model='l2' (sum of squared deviations from segment mean) is used as the default cost function.

By default, the penalty is set per participant via the BIC-style heuristic\beta = 3 \cdot \log(T) \cdot \widehat{\sigma}^2,

where T is the participant’s number of trials and \widehat{\sigma}^2 = \mathrm{Var}\!\big(\mathrm{diff}(s)\big) is a noise scale estimated from the first differences of the signal. This adapts the penalty to each participant’s own signal scale and length. Sensitivity to the penalty can be inspected by overriding via --cp_penalty <value>.

Given a participant’s set of detected change-points \{\hat{t}_k\}_{k=1}^{\hat{K}} and the set of true episode-boundary trials \{t^*_j\}_{j=1}^{J} (transitions only, episode 1 has no preceding boundary), four per-participant metrics are computed:

Per-transition signed latency is computed for each true transition t^*_j. This is the signed distance to the nearest detected change-point: \ell_j = \hat{t}_{k^*} - t^*_j, where k^* = \arg\min_k \lvert \hat{t}_k - t^*_j \rvert. Negative values are anticipatory; positive values are reactive.

Per-transition hit indicator is True if \lvert \ell_j \rvert \leq \text{tolerance} (default tolerance: 5 trials).

Per-participant hit rate is the proportion of true transitions correctly detected within tolerance.

False-alarm rate per 100 non-transition trials is the number of detected change-points not matched to any true transition within tolerance, normalised by (T - J) / 100.

Mean unsigned latency is \frac{1}{J}\sum_j \lvert \ell_j \rvert, computed over transitions where a latency is defined (NaN for transitions never matched).

The per-transition signed latency is the unit of analysis for the parametric test. A linear mixed model is fit on the long-format per-transition table:latency ~ condition_L + condition_Q
          + episode_index_c
          + condition_L : episode_index_c
          + condition_Q : episode_index_c
          + transition_dir_sum
          + condition_L : transition_dir_sum

Random effects: (1 + episode_index_c | participant_id).

The structure deliberately mirrors M5 so that interaction signs and magnitudes can be compared coefficient-by-coefficient between the two analyses (for cross-validation). Transitions where no detection occurred (NaN latency) are excluded from this model and tracked separately in the companion model below.

The target angle for episode e is computed as the circular mean of actual_vector_angle over all delivered-outcome trials in episode e. Averaging across cues produces the latent-state-induced reference (rather than a cue-specific reference), which is the relevant target for “did the participant reach the new state?”. The time-to-recovery is the smallest trial_in_episode value \geq 1 such that\big\lvert \mathrm{wrap}_{[-180°, +180°]}\!\big(\theta_t - \theta^{\text{target}}_e\big) \big\rvert \leq \text{threshold}.

If the threshold is never reached within the episode, the observation is right-censored at the episode length.

The event indicator is 1 if the threshold was reached, 0 if right-censored.

The analysis is run at two thresholds: 15° (strict) and 30° (lenient), both reported. The two thresholds are implement to represent two layered questions. The 30° threshold asks “did the participant reach the right region?” while the 15° threshold asks “did the participant consolidate tightly?”. Consistent vs divergent effects between the two thresholds could themselves be informative.

The semiparametric Cox proportional hazards model (Cox, 1972) is fit at each threshold:\lambda(t \mid x) = \lambda_0(t) \exp\!\big(\beta^\top x\big),

where x comprises:condition_L + condition_Q
+ episode_index_c
+ transition_dir_sum
+ condition_L : episode_index_c

Implementation: lifelines.CoxPHFitter (Davidson-Pilon, 2019).

Each participant contributes 7 (8! CHECK) transitions. The Cox partial likelihood treats observations as independent, which understates SEs in the presence of within-participant correlation. We use cluster-robust standard errors (Lin & Wei, 1989) with cluster_col="participant_id". This is a sandwich-type robust variance estimator analogous to those used in GEE, and is the standard alternative when frailty terms are not natively supported (which they are not in lifelines at the time of writing).( (So this is the survival-analysis analogue of the cluster-robust OLS fallback used in the GLMMs in the framework)

In the Cox model, \beta_k > 0 corresponds to a higher hazard, i.e., faster recovery (the recovery event happens sooner). The exponentiated coefficient \exp(\beta_k) is the hazard ratio per unit increase in the covariate.

The central test is condition_L (a positive coefficient means recovery is faster in higher-instruction conditions, on the unit-contrast scale).

Overall, each addresses a different facet of the same underlying construct (latent-state inference / cross-cue generalisation):



What it asks

Operationalisation

M5

At the focal first-c_2 trial, how close is the participant’s net to the new target?

Parametric, requires defining I_e and the previous-episode reference; cue-specific

M_CP

When does the participant’s trajectory show a discontinuity?

Non-parametric (PELT detection), no cue-specificity

M_SURV

How long until the participant’s net mean reaches the new target?

The three instruction conditions are the primary between-subjects manipulation in TAMBI. They vary in how much explicit structural information participants receive about the cue–direction relationships and episode transitions before the task begins.
This manipulation doesn’t just allow the comparison of learning-from-scratch with partial and complete structural knowledge, but also creates a between-condition manipulation of structural priors, representing exposure to different levels of task ambiguity.

Instruction condition is randomly assigned to each participant before the session and determines which set of instruction slides is presented by the PsychoPy script.

All participants complete the same practice trial regardless of condition. The practice is a free-exploration phase with progressive hints:

The screen coordinate system uses degrees of visual angle with the origin at the center of the screen. All slot positions are computed analytically from the angle formula:def angle_to_position(self, angle_deg, radius=8):
    angle_rad = math.radians(angle_deg)
    x = radius * math.cos(angle_rad)
    y = radius * math.sin(angle_rad)
    return [x, y]

The 32 slots are positioned at equal angular intervals (11.25° per slot) on the defense perimeter circle. Slot 0 is at 0° (3 o’clock position in standard math coordinates). The slot assignment for a mouse click uses nearest-slot logic:def get_slot_from_position(self, pos):
    min_distance = float('inf')
    closest_slot = None
    for i, slot_pos in enumerate(self.slot_positions):
        distance = math.sqrt((pos[0]-slot_pos[0])**2 + (pos[1]-slot_pos[1])**2)
        if distance < min_distance:
            min_distance = distance
            closest_slot = i
    return closest_slot if min_distance < 1.5 else None

The 1.5° threshold means that clicks far from all slots (e.g., near the center or outside the circle) are not registered.

The Mosquito Defense Task is a spatial predictive inference paradigm implemented in PsychoPy. On each trial, participants allocate up to 7 defensive nets across 32 evenly spaced angular positions on a circular perimeter, with the goal of intercepting a mosquito that will subsequently attack from a direction governed by the task’s latent structure.

The task is presented with a narrative and visual framing (described in 

Gamification and Game Design) in which the participant is a defender protecting a central resource from mosquito attacks. The spatial, circular structure of the defense problem directly embodies the angular inference problem that is the scientific focus of the study.

The central visual display consists of:

A central light cue circle that changes color each trial to indicate the active cue identity. During the anticipation phase, this cue is visible; during barrier placement, it remains visible.

A defense perimeter circle on which the 32 slots are positioned at equal angular intervals (11.25° per slot).

32 slot indicators - small white circles at each slot position indicating available placement positions.

A blood counter arc - a colored arc on an inner circle indicating the current blood point total (initially 100, updated after each outcome trial).

Net visuals - image-based net stimuli that appear at slot positions when barriers are placed.

Mouse cursor - a small red circle showing the current cursor position, accompanied by a small net image and a counter showing remaining nets.

The blood counter has no mechanical consequence in the current implementation — it does not end the experiment and does not trigger any qualitative state change. It functions purely as a continuous feedback display of cumulative performance, providing motivational salience to individual trial outcomes.

Scheduled breaks occur approximately every 40–60 trials (randomized to avoid episode boundary overlap). The break screen is displayed until the participant presses Space, after which an experimenter confirmation screen waits for the experimenter to press ‘P’ before the experiment resumes. Maximum break duration is 3 minutes. After each break, a drift correction is performed and a 3-2-1 countdown is shown before the next trial begins.

Within-task emotional state ratings are collected 1–2 times per episode. The rating is triggered at either trial 7 or trial 14 of the episode (randomly chosen per episode), but not both. If not triggered at trial 7 (50% chance), it is triggered at trial 14 by default.

The rating screen presents six continuous sliders (valence, arousal, anxiety, stress, frustration, fatigue) in randomized order. Participants drag the sliders with the mouse. The rating is confirmed by pressing Space.

Trial schedules are pre-generated as CSV files and stored in the trial_schedules/ directory. One schedule file is selected randomly at session start, ensuring that trial properties are rigorously controlled while still providing participant-level randomization. This approach avoids the risk of generating invalid schedules at runtime (e.g., constraint violations) and enables efficient session startup, ensuring low susceptibility to errors.

Each schedule file is generated by the trial_schedule_generation.ipynb notebook and encodes all trial-level information needed by the PsychoPy task: episode membership, cue color, target angle, observed angle (target + von Mises noise), outcome occurrence, and oddball flag.

This ensures controlled randomization within defined boundaries - in this way, the analysis can focus on the structural parameters of the task, while the constrained randomization (or jittering) ensures that any observed effects are not merely artifacts of a highly specific trial sequence.

The boundary constraint is the most demanding structural requirement: the last trial of each episode and the first trial of the next episode must display the same color cue. This prevents a cue switch from co-occurring with an episode transition, ensuring that the only signal of a transition is the change in attack direction.

A secondary constraint requires that:

Episodes 2–5 each begin with 3–4 consecutive trials of the cue that initiates the learning phase

The learning-phase cue identities are balanced (2 of each identity in episodes 2–5)

All 8 episode transition cues are balanced (4 of each identity)

The planning algorithm proceeds as follows:

Generate a balanced sequence of transition cue identities (4 of identity 1, 4 of identity 2, with the first 4 balanced 2:2).

For each episode, attempt to generate a valid cue sequence satisfying:

Required start color (= last color of previous episode, if available)

Required learning-phase start color (for episodes 2–5)

Maximum within-episode color streak of 3

Approximately equal representation of both colors within the episode

If any episode produces a conflict between the boundary constraint and the learning-phase identity requirement, discard the current identity sequence and retry with a new one.

This procedure is iterated up to 1000 times. In practice, a valid plan is almost always found within ~50 attempts.

After the cue sequence is determined, outcome omission trials are assigned per episode:

Valid positions for omissions exclude:

The first 4 trials of each episode (learning phase)

The last trial of each episode

Trials immediately following a cue switch

Placement algorithm:

Compute target omission count based on a random rate drawn from [5%, 15%]

Select omission positions from valid positions, avoiding consecutive omissions where possible

If strict non-consecutive selection cannot achieve the target count, allow consecutive omissions

Oddballs are assigned after omissions, with additional constraints:

Valid positions for oddballs additionally exclude:

Trials that are already omission trials

Trials immediately adjacent (±1) to omission trials

Consecutive oddball avoidance: If the target count cannot be achieved without consecutive oddballs, the target is reduced rather than allowing consecutive oddballs.

Overlap check: A validation step confirms that no trial is simultaneously an omission and an oddball. The schedule generation notebook reports the overlap count, which must be 0.

# function to add angle noise 
# Args:
#   - target_angle in degree
#   - noise_std in degree
#   - use_gaussian: True for gaussian noise, false for von Mises based noise
# Returns:
#   - angle with noise in degree (0-360) --> Stimulus angle

def add_angle_noise(target_angle, kappa_noise=kappa, use_gaussian=False):
        
    # Sample from von Mises distribution centred around target_angle
    target_rad = np.radians(target_angle)
    noisy_rad = vonmises.rvs(kappa_noise, loc=target_rad)
    noisy_angle = np.degrees(noisy_rad) % 360
    
    return noisy_angle

def generate_balanced_episode_lengths(n_episodes, base_length, min_length, max_length, target_mean_min, target_mean_max):
   
    target_total = base_length * n_episodes  # Target total trials
    
    while True:
        # Generate random lengths within the allowed range
        lengths = []
        for i in range(n_episodes):
            length = random.randint(min_length, max_length)
            lengths.append(length)
        
        # Check if the mean is within acceptable range
        actual_mean = sum(lengths) / n_episodes
        
        if target_mean_min <= actual_mean <= target_mean_max:
            return lengths
        
        # If mean is too low or too high, adjust some episodes
        if actual_mean < target_mean_min:
            # Need to increase some episodes
            deficit = target_total - sum(lengths)
            for i in range(min(deficit, n_episodes)):
                if lengths[i] < max_length:
                    lengths[i] += 1
        elif actual_mean > target_mean_max:
            # Need to decrease some episodes  
            excess = sum(lengths) - target_total
            for i in range(min(excess, n_episodes)):
                if lengths[i] > min_length:
                    lengths[i] -= 1
        
        # Check again
        actual_mean = sum(lengths) / n_episodes
        if target_mean_min <= actual_mean <= target_mean_max:
            return lengths

def assign_outcomes_per_episode(trials, min_rate=min_omission_rate, max_rate=max_omission_rate, target_overall=target_overall_omission_rate):
    
    outcomes = np.ones(len(trials))
    
    # Group trials by episode
    episodes = {}
    for i, trial in enumerate(trials):
        ep = trial['episode']
        if ep not in episodes:
            episodes[ep] = []
        episodes[ep].append(i)

    episode_rates = {}
    total_omissions_assigned = 0

    # Schritt 1: Für jede Episode exakte Anzahl basierend auf Episode-Rate bestimmen
    for episode_num, trial_indices in episodes.items():
        episode_length = len(trial_indices)
        
        # Zufällige Rate innerhalb der erlaubten Grenzen
        episode_rate = random.uniform(min_rate, max_rate)
        target_omissions = round(episode_length * episode_rate)
        
        # Strikt innerhalb min/max bounds halten
        min_allowed = max(1, round(episode_length * min_rate))
        max_allowed = round(episode_length * max_rate)
        target_omissions = max(min_allowed, min(max_allowed, target_omissions))

        # Valide Positionen bestimmen
        valid_indices = []
        for i in trial_indices:
            trial = trials[i]
            if trial['trial_in_episode'] <= 4:   # learning phase
                continue
            if trial['trial_in_episode'] == trial['episode_length']:  # last trial
                continue
            if i > 0 and trials[i]['cue_color'] != trials[i-1]['cue_color']:  # cue switch
                continue
            valid_indices.append(i)

        # Anzahl an verfügbare Positionen anpassen falls nötig
        if len(valid_indices) < target_omissions:
            print(f"[Warnung] Episode {episode_num}: nur {len(valid_indices)} gültige Positionen "
                  f"für {target_omissions} gewünschte Omissions")
            target_omissions = len(valid_indices)

        # Deterministische Auswahl ohne consecutive
        random.shuffle(valid_indices)
        selected = []
        for candidate in valid_indices:
            if all(abs(candidate - s) > 1 for s in selected):
                selected.append(candidate)
            if len(selected) >= target_omissions:
                break

        # Falls nicht genug non-consecutive Positionen verfügbar, fülle mit beliebigen auf
        if len(selected) < target_omissions:
            remaining_valid = [idx for idx in valid_indices if idx not in selected]
            needed = target_omissions - len(selected)
            random.shuffle(remaining_valid)
            selected.extend(remaining_valid[:needed])

        # Omissions setzen
        for idx in selected:
            outcomes[idx] = 0

        total_omissions_assigned += len(selected)
        actual_rate = len(selected) / episode_length if episode_length > 0 else 0
        episode_rates[episode_num] = actual_rate

        print(f"Episode {episode_num}: Ziel={target_omissions}, "
              f"gesetzt={len(selected)}, "
              f"Rate={actual_rate:.2%} (min={min_rate:.2%}, max={max_rate:.2%})")

    # Finale Statistiken
    overall_rate = total_omissions_assigned / len(trials)
    print(f"\n[Final] Gesamt: {total_omissions_assigned}/{len(trials)} "
          f"= {overall_rate:.2%}, Ziel={target_overall:.2%}")

    return outcomes, episode_rates, overall_rate

        target_oddballs = max(min_possible, min(max_possible, target_oddballs))

    # Schritt 2: oddballs tatsächlich zuweisen (ohne globales Balancing)
    for episode_num, trial_indices in episodes.items():

        # Zufällige Rate innerhalb der erlaubten Grenzen

        # Strikt innerhalb min/max bounds halten

        valid_indices = []
        for i in trial_indices:
            trial = trials[i]
            if trial['trial_in_episode'] <= 4:   # learning phase
                continue
            if trial['trial_in_episode'] == trial['episode_length']:  # letztes Trial
                continue
            if i > 0 and trials[i]['cue_color'] != trials[i-1]['cue_color']:  # cue switch
                continue
            if outcomes[i] == 0:  # bereits outcome omission
                continue
            if i+1 < len(outcomes) and outcomes[i+1] == 0:  # nächstes Trial ist outcome omission
                continue
            if i-1 >= 0 and outcomes[i-1] == 0:  # vorheriges Trial ist outcome omission
                continue
            valid_indices.append(i)

        if len(valid_indices) < target_oddballs:

        # deterministische Auswahl ohne consecutive
        random.shuffle(valid_indices)
        selected = []
        for candidate in valid_indices:
            if all(abs(candidate - s) > 1 for s in selected):
                selected.append(candidate)
            if len(selected) >= target_oddballs:
                break

        # Falls nicht genug non-consecutive Positionen verfügbar, versuche weniger strikt
        if len(selected) < target_oddballs:
            remaining_valid = [idx for idx in valid_indices if idx not in selected]
            needed = target_oddballs - len(selected)
            
            # Versuche erst noch non-consecutive zu finden
            for candidate in remaining_valid:
                if all(abs(candidate - s) > 1 for s in selected) and len(selected) < target_oddballs:
                    selected.append(candidate)
            
            # Falls immer noch nicht genug, reduziere das Ziel anstatt consecutive zu erlauben
            if len(selected) < target_oddballs:
                print(f"[Info] Episode {episode_num}: Reduziere Oddball-Ziel von {target_oddballs} auf {len(selected)} "
                      f"um consecutive Oddballs zu vermeiden")
                target_oddballs = len(selected)

        for idx in selected:
            oddballs[idx] = 1

        total_oddballs_assigned += len(selected)

        print(f"Episode {episode_num}: Oddball Ziel={target_oddballs}, "
              f"gesetzt={len(selected)}, "
              f"Rate={actual_rate:.2%} (min={min_rate:.2%}, max={max_rate:.2%})")

    # Finale Statistiken ohne globales Balancing
    total_oddballs = int(np.sum(oddballs))
    overall_rate = total_oddballs / len(trials)

    print(f"\n[Final Oddball] Gesamt: {total_oddballs}/{len(trials)} "
          f"= {overall_rate:.2%}, Ziel={target_overall:.2%}")

    return oddballs, episode_rates, overall_rate

def generate_valid_cue_sequence(n_trials, required_start_color=None, required_end_color=None, episode_num=1, learning_phase_trials=0):
    
    for attempt in range(max_sequence_attempts):
        # Calculate number of trials per color (approximately half each -> 10 +/- 2 on average)
        n_color1 = random.randint(max(1, n_trials//2 - 2), min(n_trials-1, n_trials//2 + 2))
        n_color2 = n_trials - n_color1
        
        counts = {cue_colors[0]: 0, cue_colors[1]: 0}
        sequence = []
        
        # Handle learning phase trials at the start
        learning_trials_added = 0
        if learning_phase_trials > 0 and required_start_color:
            for i in range(min(learning_phase_trials, n_trials)):
                sequence.append(required_start_color)
                counts[required_start_color] += 1
                learning_trials_added += 1
        
        # Fill remaining positions
        remaining_positions = n_trials - learning_trials_added
        if required_end_color and remaining_positions > 0:
            remaining_positions -= 1  
        
        # Calculate remaining quota for each color
        remaining_color1 = n_color1 - counts[cue_colors[0]]
        remaining_color2 = n_color2 - counts[cue_colors[1]]
        
        # Adjust if end color requirement affects quota
        if required_end_color:
            if required_end_color == cue_colors[0]:
                remaining_color1 -= 1
            else:
                remaining_color2 -= 1
        
        # Generate middle section randomly while respecting quotas and streak limits
        temp_counts = {cue_colors[0]: remaining_color1, cue_colors[1]: remaining_color2}
        
        for pos in range(remaining_positions):
            available_colors = [c for c in cue_colors if temp_counts[c] > 0]
            
            # Enforce max streak constraint
            if len(sequence) >= max_same_color_streak:
                if all(color == sequence[-1] for color in sequence[-max_same_color_streak:]):
                    if sequence[-1] in available_colors:
                        available_colors.remove(sequence[-1])
            
            if not available_colors:
                break  # Failed this attempt, try again
            
            chosen_color = random.choice(available_colors)
            sequence.append(chosen_color)
            temp_counts[chosen_color] -= 1
        
        # Add required end color if specified
        if required_end_color and len(sequence) == n_trials - 1:
            sequence.append(required_end_color)
            counts[required_end_color] += 1
        
        # Verify the sequence meets all requirements
        if (len(sequence) == n_trials and 
            sequence.count(cue_colors[0]) == n_color1 and 
            sequence.count(cue_colors[1]) == n_color2 and
            (not required_start_color or sequence[0] == required_start_color) and
            (not required_end_color or sequence[-1] == required_end_color)):
            return sequence
    
    raise Exception(f"Could not generate valid sequence for episode {episode_num} after {max_sequence_attempts} attempts")

This guide will walk through building a MyST site, scrubbing source files, encrypting the HTML with a password, and deploying it to a separate public GitHub Pages repository - all automated via GitHub Actions.

You will need two repositories:

The Source Repo (private): contains your .md files, figures and/or other assets, myst.yml, toc.yml and optinally additional scripts to control the design etc.. (e.g. the repo your-username/study_documentation)

The Public Website Repo: will only contain the encrypted HTML output. (e.g., your-username/study-website)

records.content:
Go to GitHub and create a new repository.

Name it appropriately (e.g. tambi-website).

Do not initialize it with a README, .gitignore, or license. Leave it completely empty.
Your workflow needs two secrets to function: one for the website password, and one to grant permission to push to the public repository.

records.content:
Because the workflow pushes code from your source repo to a different repository, the default GITHUB_TOKEN isn’t enough. You need a PAT.

Go to GitHub → Settings → Developer settings → Personal access tokens → Tokens (classic).

Click Generate new token (classic).

Give it a name (e.g., Deploy Docs Token).

Under scopes, check repo (Full control of private repositories).

Click Generate token and copy the token immediately (you won’t see it again).

records.content:
Go to your Source Repo (e.g. tambi_documentation).

Go to Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions.

Click New repository secret.

Name: DEPLOY_TOKEN

Value: Paste the PAT you just created.

Click Add secret.

Click New repository secret again.

Name: STATICRYPT_PASSWORD

Value: Choose the password you want visitors to type to access the website.

Click Add secret.
Now you’ll create the automated GitHub Actions workflow in your source repository.

In your source repo, create a file at .github/workflows/build-and-encrypt.yml.

Paste the following code into it:name: Build and Encrypt Site

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - name: Checkout Private Source Code
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Setup Node.js
        uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '20'

      - name: Install MyST and Staticrypt
        run: npm install -g mystmd staticrypt

      - name: Build MyST Site
        env:
          BASE_URL: /tambi-website/ # ⚠️ CHANGE THIS to match your public repo name!
        run: myst build --html

      - name: Scrub Source Files and Service Worker
        run: |
          echo "Deleting Service Worker..."
          rm -f ./_build/html/service-worker.js

          echo "Finding and deleting source Markdown files..."
          find ./_build/html -name "*.md" -type f -print -delete

          echo "Finding and deleting Notebook files..."
          find ./_build/html -name "*.ipynb" -type f -print -delete

          echo "Verification — any .md files remaining?"
          REMAINING=$(find ./_build/html -name "*.md" -type f)
          if [ -n "$REMAINING" ]; then
            echo "❌ WARNING: .md files still exist:"
            echo "$REMAINING"
          else
            echo "✅ No .md files remaining."
          fi

      - name: Encrypt HTML Files
        env:
          STATICRYPT_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.STATICRYPT_PASSWORD }}
        run: |
          if [ -z "${STATICRYPT_PASSWORD}" ]; then
            echo "❌ STATICRYPT_PASSWORD is EMPTY! Check your secret name."
            exit 1
          fi
          echo "✅ Password is set (length: ${#STATICRYPT_PASSWORD})"

          echo "Starting encryption..."
          FAILED=0
          while read -r file; do
            # Create a unique temp directory for this file's output
            TMPDIR=$(mktemp -d)

            # Encrypt the file — output goes to $TMPDIR/<filename>
            # Note: staticrypt v3 does not have an -o flag, must use -d
            if ! staticrypt "$file" -p "${STATICRYPT_PASSWORD}" -d "$TMPDIR"; then
              echo "❌ staticrypt failed for: $file"
              FAILED=1
              rm -rf "$TMPDIR"
              continue
            fi

            # Find the encrypted output file
            ENCRYPTED_FILE="$TMPDIR/$(basename "$file")"

            if [ -f "$ENCRYPTED_FILE" ]; then
              # Overwrite the original with the encrypted version
              cp "$ENCRYPTED_FILE" "$file"
              echo "✅ Encrypted: $file"
            else
              echo "❌ Encrypted file not found for: $file"
              FAILED=1
            fi

            rm -rf "$TMPDIR"
          done < <(find ./_build/html -name "*.html")

          if [ "$FAILED" -eq 1 ]; then
            echo "Encryption FAILED for one or more files."
            exit 1
          fi

          echo "Encryption complete."

      - name: Final Verification Before Deploy
        run: |
          echo "=== Checking for leaked source files ==="
          LEAKED=false

          MD_FILES=$(find ./_build/html -name "*.md" -type f)
          if [ -n "$MD_FILES" ]; then
            echo "❌ .md files found:"
            echo "$MD_FILES"
            LEAKED=true
          fi

          IPYNB_FILES=$(find ./_build/html -name "*.ipynb" -type f)
          if [ -n "$IPYNB_FILES" ]; then
            echo "❌ .ipynb files found:"
            echo "$IPYNB_FILES"
            LEAKED=true
          fi

          if [ "$LEAKED" = true ]; then
            echo "❌ Source files would be leaked! Aborting deploy."
            exit 1
          else
            echo "✅ No source files found. Safe to deploy."
          fi

          echo "=== Checking encryption ==="
          if head -n 5 ./_build/html/index.html | grep -qi "staticrypt"; then
            echo "✅ index.html is encrypted."
          else
            echo "❌ index.html is NOT encrypted!"
            exit 1
          fi

      - name: Deploy to Public Repo
        uses: peaceiris/actions-gh-pages@v3
        with:
          publish_dir: ./_build/html
          external_repository: your-username/tambi-website # ⚠️ CHANGE THIS to your public repo!
          publish_branch: main
          personal_token: ${{ secrets.DEPLOY_TOKEN }}
          force_orphan: true

⚠️ Make two changes in the file:

Change BASE_URL: /tambi-website/ to match your public repository name (e.g., /my-docs-site/).

Change external_repository: your-username/tambi-website to the full name of your public repository.

Commit the file to the main branch.

Go to your Public Website Repository (e.g., tambi-website).

Go to Settings → Pages.

Under “Build and deployment”, set Source to Deploy from a branch.

Set Branch to main and folder to / (root).

Click Save.

Make a small change to your source repository (like adding a space to a markdown file) and push it to main.

Go to the Actions tab in your source repository.

Watch the workflow run. It should pass all checks, including the ✅ No source files found and ✅ index.html is encrypted steps.

Once complete, go to https://your-username.github.io/tambi-website/ (replace with your repo name).

You should be greeted by a StatiCrypt password prompt! Enter the password you set in the STATICRYPT_PASSWORD secret to view your documentation.

You’re done! Now, every time you push changes to your private source repository, GitHub Actions will automatically build it, scrub the source files, encrypt the HTML, and deploy the secure version to your public website.
